reason: Attacked and survived. I went after three things and got none of them. WORDING AND PLACEMENT: rather than read a summary of the page, I downloaded the chapter itself and looked at the raw markup. The paragraph reads Freedom only for the supporters of the government, only for the members of one party, however numerous they may be, is no freedom at all. Freedom is always and exclusively freedom for the one who thinks differently. Not because of any fanatical concept of justice but because all that is instructive, wholesome and purifying in political freedom depends on this essential characteristic, and its effectiveness vanishes when freedom becomes a special privilege. The card's sentence is that, character for character, with its own terminal stop, and it is in a body paragraph: I checked the markup around it precisely because this sentence is often said to live in a footnote or a marginal note of the manuscript, and in the Wolfe text it does not, it is running text. The quotation also stops where Wolfe's sentence stops and does not run into the fanatical concept of justice clause, which would have changed the sense. TRANSLATION: the archive's index page for the work states the edition in its own fields, Written 1918, First Published 1922 by Paul Levi, Source The Russian Revolution by Rosa Luxemburg, Publisher Workers Age Publishers New York 1940, Translated Bertram Wolfe. So the translator named on the card is the translator of the text read, which is the failure mode this track worries about most, and here it is closed. Bertram D. Wolfe is his standard form and is not an embellishment. LOCATOR: the same index page lists the contents in order, and The Problem of Dictatorship is the sixth title, so ch. 6 and the chapter name on the card both check out, and the passage is in that chapter's argument about freedom under one party, where the card says. ATTRIBUTION AND THE REST: Luxemburg's own manuscript prose, not reported and not a character, so no speaker is owed, and the misattribution list carries no Luxemburg trap. shipped.js returns no shipped hit, no near-hit, puts her at 1 of 3 for the year from February and reports her not banned and not at cap; carry.json holds no Luxemburg and no second Luxemburg appears in June's verdicts, so one person a month is safe. Scope: written 1918, published 1922, translated 1940, all before 1999. It is a written manuscript, not a speech, so the oratory exclusion does not touch it, and political philosophy is philosophy, which the track has already accepted by landing a Luxemburg line in February. Publishable: it is an argument about dissent with nothing graphic in it. Theme fit is strong and is a clarity line rather than a counsel line, which suits six in the morning. Source line form: leads with Rosa Luxemburg, no dash, no straight double quote, 106 characters. I could not break it.

residual: Two things for the editor rather than the refuter. The tag: The Russian Revolution is a political pamphlet, so Essay is arguable as the form, though Philosophy is defensible for political theory and does not misdescribe it. And the sentence is famous enough to be used as a slogan detached from its argument; the card does not need a note, but if June wants one, the honest one says Luxemburg is writing about a revolution she supported, which is what makes the line cost her something.
